candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XVIII.1. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And the Lord appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre... behold, three men stood by him'. Ephrem reads the three visitors as a Trinitarian theophany — the Lord (singular) who appears IS the three (plural). Tewahedo iconography preserves the Mamre-Trinity tradition most fully of any major Christian communion (the Andrew Rublev icon tradition is Slavonic; the Tewahedo iconographic Trinity-at-Mamre is older and more widespread in church-wall fresco than in any other Oriental Orthodox communion). Ephrem's exegesis is the Patristic foundation.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XVIII.14. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Is any thing too hard for the Lord?' Ephrem reads the rhetorical question as the FOUNDATIONAL apologetic for divine omnipotence — and specifically for miracle-faith against rational doubt. The Tewahedo annunciation reading explicitly draws on Gen 18:14 (Sarah's incredulity → Isaac's miraculous birth) as the OT type of Lk 1:37 ('for with God nothing shall be impossible' — the angel to Mary). Ephrem's exegesis pins the typological chain.
